About the experiment 
Independent variable 
Percent of sphagnum moss added to the pots, except for the control with 100% regolith 
Dependent variable 
Plant growth: 
- height 
- number of leaves 
- number of pods 
- number of flowers 
Controls 
1.​ Ratio of moss vs regolith (pot 1 - 100% lunar regolith; pot 2 - 50% regolith and 50% 
sphagnum moss; pot 3 - 75% regolith and 25% sphagnum moss; pot 4 - 85% regolith 
and 15% sphagnum moss). 
2.​ Pot size (provided by PTMC Jr). 
3.​ Species of plant (beans/Phaseolus vulgaris L.). 
4.​ Water amount (all pots received the same amount of water per watering). 
5.​ Type of water: filtered tap water. 
6.​ Number of seeds per pot (3 seeds added to each pot). 
7.​ Temperature (depended a lot on the temperature in our house and the weather). 
8.​ Humidity (was not the same throughout the experiment because it depended on the 
humidity of our home, but was the same for all pots). 
9.​ Light (It was kept constant for all of the plants but depended on local climate. Curtains 
were scheduled to open at sunrise and close at sunset using Aqara Home). 
Amendments 
For this experiment we used New Zealand sphagnum moss (typically used for orchids). It has 
the unique ability to absorb up to 20 times its own weight in water. 
Hypothesis 
The amount of sphagnum moss we add will distribute the water more evenly throughout the pot 
and lead to more efficient plant growth. It will also make the soil less compacted, which might 
result in higher plants, more leaves, flowers, and pods. 
1

Team name: Lunar Planting 
Team ID: 22975 
Background 
Why Lunar regolith? 
NASA’s Artemis missions inspired me to choose Lunar regolith for my experiment. Contributing 
to the success of this mission will open doors for further space exploration and colonization. 
Why sphagnum moss? 
Sphagnum moss has the property of absorbing up to 20 times its own weight in water, which 
means less frequent watering will be needed, saving one of the most precious resources in 
space. It also has the ability to reduce the compaction of lunar regolith. Sphagnum moss is 
lightweight, reducing the cost of the payload. Last but not least, when shagnum moss 
decomposes it also adds organic matter to the potting medium. 
Why plant growth (flowers, leaves, pods, etc.)? 
We monitor the number of leaves as more leaves means more photosynthesis, therefore more 
food for the plant to produce pods. We counted the number of flowers to see how many pods 
one plant might produce in the regolith. We counted the number of pods to see how many of the 
flowers produced pods. 
Why beans? 
Beans are very nutritious and filling, therefore a good meal source for astronauts in space. The 
specific kind of bean I selected contains the following nutrients and minerals per 100 grams: 
21.3 g of protein, 1.8 g of fat, 40 g of carbohydrates, 17 g of fiber, 0.50 mg vitamin B1, 140 mg 
of magnesium, 0.01 mg of sodium, 426 mg of phosphorus, 6.17 mg of iron, 2.6 mg of zinc, and 
the energy value is 260 kcal 
Furthermore, they are self-pollinating, which means they will not require pollinators to be 
brought to space; they are nitrogen fixers, meaning that the potting mix they grow in will be 
beneficial for the next crop that will be planted there; their stalks and leaves can be turned into 
compost, which will add organic material and enrich the soil. 
Beans also have a relatively fast period from sowing to cropping: between 45 to 75 days. Dried 
beans can be stored for longer periods of time, allowing the astronauts to cook them whenever 
needed and bringing variety to their diet. 
Experimental rational 
My experiment brings astronauts in space a good source of nutrition, the first steps for 
cultivating Mars and the Moon. This has relevance because my discoveries could potentially 
bring the Artemis missions valuable data and ideas.

Grow pot setup 
 
Four pots were prepared and planted: 
Pot 1 - 100% regolith (control) 
Pot 2 - 50% regolith, 50% sphagnum moss 
Pot 3 - 75% regolith, 25% sphagnum moss 
Pot 4 - 85% regolith, 15% sphagnum moss 
 
Ammendments: 
Premium 
New Zealand 
Sphagnum moss (as described above) 
 
Crop: White bean variety from Dobrudzha, 
Bulgaria, often referred to as Dobruzhanka. 
 
 
Procedures: 
Planting procedure: 
1.​ Presoak the beans overnight 
2.​ Take out 4 pots and label them 
3.​ Divide the height of pots according to the percentage of regolith to be added (100%, 
85%, 75%, 50%) 
4.​ Take pot 1, fill with 100% regolith, place the regolith in a separate container, moisten the 
regolith, return potting mix to the pot and set aside for sowing. 
5.​ Take pot 2, fill with 50% regolith, add 50% sphagnum moss, place mixture in a separate 
container, mix and moisten, return potting mix to the pot and set aside for sowing. 
6.​ Take pot 3, fill with 75% regolith, add 25% spahgnum moss, place mixture in a separate 
container, mix and moisten, return potting mix to the pot and set aside for sowing. 
7.​ Take pot 4, fill with 85% regolith, add 15% sphagnum moss, place mixture in a separate 
container, mix and moisten, return potting mix to the pot and set aside for sowing. 
8.​ Sow 3 seeds of equal size in each of the pots. 
9.​ Place the pots next to the window receiving the most light in our living room.

Number of pods 
During the last week, pots 2 and 4 both had 1.5 pods on average. 
Analysis 
The experimental design was sound and the collected data is trustworthy and consistent. 
However, the failure of the first planting in pot 1 and the shorter growth period for the team (1 
week was lost due to illness) did not produce the convincing results we were hoping for. 
By height, the 75% regolith, 25% sphagnum moss pot achieved the best results, however it did 
not grow any pods before the end of the growth period. For comparison, pot 2 and pot 4 did not 
reach the same average height, but at the end of the growth period each of them had 1.5 pods 
on average.

What we have observed for all 3 plants in pot 4 (85% regolith) is that its leaves gradually started 
to yellow from the bottom up, as you will see from the graph “Average Number of Leaves Per 
Pot”. This might be considered evidence of a shorter life span for the plants in the lunar regolith. 
However, further experiments should be conducted in order to reach a conclusion. 
Conclusions 
We believe that adding sphagnum moss could be beneficial, especially for high water demand 
plants on the moon. However, from our experiment we could not fully conclude what the best 
ratio of sphagnum moss for bean plants is. Further experiments should be done in order to 
determine the precise ratios that would benefit the plants the most. 
Future considerations 
1.​ Planting on the first possible day in order to give the plants enough time to grow 
2.​ Adding compost/soil to the pots that are not a control 
3.​ Thinning out the plants so the roots have more space to develop and have more 
nutrients 
4.​ Counting the total number of flowers that a plant produces instead of how many are 
currently on the plant 
5.​ Adding plant support before placing the seeds in the pots to prevent risk of damaging
